title: Small Generalizable Prompt Predictive Models Can Steer Efficient RL Post-Training of Large Reasoning Models
claim: A generalizable predictor feeds a unified batch-selection utility that steers RL training, replacing per-prompt predictors with one shared model.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, feedback loop arrow along bottom
description: A three-column framework diagram read left to right. The left column has two stacked boxes. The top, hatched box is labeled Prompt-Specific PPM. It shows candidate prompts each passing through a separate magnifier/checklist icon to give predictions. The bottom blue box is labeled Generalizable PPM. It shows the same candidates going through one shared neural network with parameters φ, ψ, η and history H_{t-1}. Arrows from both boxes enter the middle purple panel, Unified Prompt Batch Selection. That panel has a bar chart with a (γ̂−0.5)² difficulty score for prompt-wise difficulty. Below it, a plus sign leads to a cloud diagram for batch-level diversity with intra-batch and inter-step links. These combine into a Unified Batch Utility. The right green panel, RL Post-Training, shows the prompt batch going through an LLM with a reward function to give rollouts and rewards. A long arrow along the bottom loops back to update the PPM and its history.
caption: Framework overview. Unlike prompt-specific modeling like MoPPS [ref], GPS proposes a generalizable prompt predictive model (PPM) to estimate difficulty and track LLM evolution. The comprehensive prompt batch acquisition accounts for intermediate difficulty prioritization and batch-level diversity, improving RL post-training efficiency while mitigating PPM overfitting.
abstract: Reinforcement learning enhances the reasoning capabilities of large language models but often involves high computational costs due to rollout-intensive optimization. Online prompt selection presents a plausible solution by prioritizing informative prompts to improve training efficiency. However, current methods either depend on costly, exact evaluations or construct prompt-specific predictive models lacking generalization across prompts. This study introduces Generalizable Predictive Prompt Selection (GPS), which performs Bayesian inference towards prompt difficulty using a lightweight generative model trained on the shared optimization history. Intermediate-difficulty prioritization and history-anchored diversity are incorporated into the batch acquisition principle to select informative prompt batches. The small predictive model also generalizes at test-time for efficient computational allocation. Experiments across varied reasoning benchmarks indicate GPS's substantial improvements in training efficiency, final performance, and test-time efficiency over superior baseline methods.
